title: Which animals (Leviticus 11)
hookLine: land animals that chew the cud and have split hooves, fish with fins and scales

cards: A puzzle. Cow: yes. Sheep: yes.
Goat, deer: yes. Pig: no. Camel: no.
Rabbit: no. Salmon: yes. Tuna: yes.
Shrimp: no. Lobster: no. Catfish: no.

teach.h: SPLIT HOOVES AND CHEWING THE CUD.
teach.b: For land animals, Leviticus eleven says: "Whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is wholly cloven-footed, and cheweth the cud, among the beasts, that may ye eat."
Two signs: split hooves, and chewing the cud, bringing food back up to chew it again, like cows, sheep, goats and deer. It needs both. The Torah names the well-known exceptions.
The camel chews the cud, but its hoof isn't split the way the verse requires. The pig has split hooves but doesn't chew the cud. One sign each, so neither is eaten.
In the water: "whatsoever hath fins and scales" may be eaten. Salmon and tuna, yes. Shellfish, with neither, no.
Catfish, no scales, no. Birds get no signs, just a list of those not eaten, which in English translations includes vultures, ravens, hawks and owls.
The old Hebrew names are hard to identify now, so Jews who keep kosher eat only birds with a long tradition of being eaten, like chicken, duck and turkey.
Insects are nearly all forbidden, though the Torah permits certain locusts, and some Yemenite Jews still keep a tradition of which ones. Now, why? The Torah doesn't say.

teach.h: THE TORAH GIVES NO HEALTH REASON.
teach.b: Maimonides suggested health reasons; others, like Abarbanel, disagreed, and some say the point is that the Torah simply doesn't explain. What it does say is: be holy.
The rules create a daily pause, a difference between what's chosen and what's passed over.
And since packaged food can hide ingredients, people who keep kosher read labels closely and look for a symbol from a supervising agency.

how: Jews who keep kosher eat mammals with split hooves that chew the cud, fish with fins and scales, and birds with a tradition of being eaten, and check packaged foods for a kosher supervision symbol.

o: signs like split hooves and fins that mark food as permitted
animals forbidden because they carry disease or dirt
animals set aside for offerings at the Temple altar

games.q: which sign is missing — tap the pairs.
p: chews the cud, hoof not split
split hooves, doesn't chew the cud

s: the Torah forbids pork for health reasons
the Torah gives no reason. Maimonides suggested health; others disagreed.
a land animal needs both signs to be eaten
split hooves and chewing the cud; one alone isn't enough.
and some Yemenite Jews still keep a tradition of which ones.

games.q: you're reading Leviticus 11 and trying to figure out if a fish is kosher. what do you check for?
o: that it lives in fresh water.
that it has fins and scales.
games.why: whatsoever hath fins and scales may be eaten. that's the whole rule for fish.

practice: If something packaged is nearby, pick it up and read the label slowly, every ingredient, even the ones you can't pronounce. If not, picture the last thing you bought. Either way, let the reading be a small act of attention.

wordCard.voice: Which animals. Land animals with split hooves that chew the cud, fish with fins and scales, and a list of birds: the Torah's signs for what may be eaten.

orig.note: Hebrew: fins and scales, the signs of a kosher fish (Leviticus 11:9).

carryVoice: Your line: read the label. What goes in is worth knowing. That's day one hundred forty-five.
